question.text: Per Chapter 9, Venture Debt differs from traditional bank debt in which of these ways?

answer.text: VD has longer tenure (10+ years) and lower coupon than bank debt.
VD is only available for listed large-cap companies.
VD is always unsecured and subordinated to all bank debt.
VD has shorter tenure (2-3 years), often includes share/collateral (including founder shares), is senior to equity in the capital structure, and typically carries an equity kicker.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 9: 'The benefits to venture debt providers are — (a) it has a contractual maturity date with shorter duration such as 2-3 years as compared to venture capital, (b) it often has shares or other collateral, and (c) it is senior to the equity in the capital structure.' Plus 'usually carry an equity kicker'. The Trap: Option A inverts the tenure. Option C mis-states VD as always subordinated — per Chapter 9, VD sits senior to equity (though junior to senior bank debt). Option B contradicts VD's start-up focus. Cross-Exam Context: XV tests VD-instrument economics. XIX-A tests concept. XIX-C all-cat covered this. Manager's Pro-Tip: Negotiate a 'cash sweep' covenant: if the borrower raises any equity round > INR X crore, Y% of proceeds must prepay the VD. This accelerates exit and recycles fund capital into new deals — critical for a 4-5 year Cat II debt AIF tenure.
